topics.title: Douglas and the first fear of water

learn.hook: A future judge of the most powerful court in the USA was once a skinny boy who froze in a swimming pool. This is his true story.
points: Author: William O. Douglas, a Judge of the US Supreme Court and an environmentalist. 'Deep Water' is an extract from his autobiography 'Of Men and Mountains'.
Form: an autobiographical, first-person account of a childhood fear of water and how he conquered it.
First fear: at three or four, on a California beach with his father, the waves knocked him down and swept over him; he was buried in water and frightened.
At ten or eleven he decided to learn to swim at the YMCA pool in Yakima, because it was safer than the river his mother warned him about. He used water wings at first.
The pool's shallow end was about three feet deep; the deep end was about nine feet.

example.q: Why did Douglas choose the YMCA pool and not the Yakima River?
steps: His mother kept warning him that the river was treacherous.
The pool was considered safe, with a shallow end of about three feet.
So the YMCA pool was the sensible place to begin.
example.answer: The river was dangerous and his mother warned him against it, while the YMCA pool was safe.

learn.reallife: Many Indian children first learn to swim in a municipal pool, often with floats like Douglas's water wings, before trying rivers or the sea, which are much less predictable.

topics.title: The misadventure at the YMCA pool

learn.hook: A big boy's idea of a joke at a swimming pool can leave a scar of fear for years.
points: A big bruiser of a boy, about eighteen, called him 'Skinny', picked him up and tossed him into the deep end.
Douglas swallowed water and sank. On the way down he planned to make a big jump from the bottom, come up and paddle to the edge.
The nine feet felt like ninety. He rose slowly and sank again; this happened three times.
Stark terror: his legs felt paralysed, he tried to scream but no sound came out, and he saw only yellowish water.
At last he stopped struggling, felt calm and peaceful, and blacked out. He woke up lying beside the pool, vomiting.

example.q: Trace the change in Douglas's state of mind while he was drowning.
steps: First: frightened but still able to plan a jump from the bottom.
Then: panic and terror as the plan failed and his legs froze.
Finally: he stopped struggling, felt peace, and blacked out.
example.answer: Fear with a plan, then sheer panic and terror, then calm peace before he lost consciousness.

learn.reallife: Lifeguards in Indian pools are trained to watch for 'silent drowning': a drowning person often cannot shout, just as Douglas could not scream.

topics.title: A fear that stayed, and a teacher with a rope

learn.hook: Some fears pass in a day. Douglas's lasted for years, until he decided enough was enough.
points: A haunting fear of water stayed with him for years; whenever he entered water, his legs would freeze and terror would grip him.
It spoiled his joys: whenever he waded in the Tieton or the Bumping River, or bathed in Warm Lake, terror gripped him; it also ruined his fishing trips and the fun of canoeing, boating and swimming.
He resolved to conquer the fear because it was ruining his enjoyment of life.
He hired an instructor who trained him for months, five days a week, an hour a day.
The method: a belt around his waist, attached to a rope that ran through a pulley on an overhead cable. The instructor held the rope and walked him back and forth across the pool.

example.q: Why did Douglas finally decide to hire an instructor?
steps: The fear stopped him from canoeing, bathing and fishing.
It was ruining the fun of outdoor life he loved.
So he resolved to overcome it with expert help.
example.answer: Because his fear was spoiling activities he loved, like canoeing and fishing, he resolved to conquer it.

learn.reallife: Indian swimming coaches still use similar methods, like a rope or a pole held by the coach, so that a frightened learner feels safe while building skill.

topics.title: Building a swimmer, piece by piece

learn.hook: Big skills are built from small parts. Douglas's instructor broke swimming into tiny steps.
points: Step-by-step training: put the face under water and exhale; raise the nose and inhale; repeat many times.
Next: hold the side of the pool and kick with the legs; then combine arms, legs and breathing into a whole stroke. 'Piece by piece he built a swimmer.'
Even after training, small traces of terror returned when he swam alone, so he kept swimming to beat them.
Test 1: at Lake Wentworth in New Hampshire, he dived off a dock and swam two miles across the lake. The terror tried to return once, but he swam on.
Test 2: at Warm Lake he dived in, swam across to the other shore and back, and shouted with joy. The terror was gone.

example.q: Why did Douglas test himself at Lake Wentworth and Warm Lake after the training?
steps: The instructor's work was done, but traces of fear remained.
He needed to be sure he could swim alone in deep, open water.
Swimming across and back at Warm Lake proved the terror was gone.
example.answer: To be sure the last traces of fear had gone, he swam alone in open lakes; at Warm Lake he knew he had won.

learn.reallife: Cricketers practise in nets ball by ball before facing a real match. Douglas did the same with breathing, kicking and strokes before facing open lakes.

topics.title: Themes: fear, the will to live and freedom

learn.hook: 'All we have to fear is fear itself.' Douglas borrowed a president's words to sum up a boy's victory.
points: Fear can paralyse a person, but it can be overcome by willpower, patience and practice.
Douglas quotes US President Franklin D. Roosevelt: 'All we have to fear is fear itself.' The fear of something is often worse than the thing.
Near death he felt peace; afterwards his will to live grew stronger. He says there is terror only in the fear of death.
Victory over fear brings freedom: he could enjoy rivers, lakes and mountains again.

example.q: Explain 'All we have to fear is fear itself' with reference to Douglas.
steps: The real enemy was not water but his fear of water.
That fear froze his legs and spoiled his life for years.
Once he faced and beat the fear, the water held no danger for him.
example.answer: His fear, not the water, was his real enemy; by conquering it, he was free.

learn.reallife: Top Indian athletes often talk about beating nerves before a big final. Mastering the fear is often the real contest.

remember: 'All we have to fear is fear itself' – Franklin D. Roosevelt
Terror is only in the fear of death
Will to live grew stronger
traps: Douglas did not feel terror right up to death
The lesson is not that swimming is dangerous

topics.title: Craft and vocabulary of Deep Water

learn.hook: Read the drowning scene and you almost hold your breath. That is the power of sensory writing.
points: Sensory description: yellowish water, choking, frozen legs; repetition of going down and coming up builds suspense.
Tone: reflective; the adult Douglas looks back calmly. Strong contrast between helplessness in the pool and triumph at Warm Lake.

Vocabulary: bruiser (big, tough person), flailed (waved wildly), paralysed (unable to move), misadventure (unlucky accident), stark terror (sheer fear), vestiges of fear (small traces), residual doubt (doubt that remains).
Think as you read: the 'misadventure' is being thrown into the deep end; he planned to spring up from the bottom; the experience left him with a fear of water for years.
Extract-based MCQs often ask about the meaning of a phrase, the narrator's feeling, or a device in the drowning scene.

example.q: Extract (paraphrased): He thrashed wildly at the surface, gulped water and choked; his legs would not rise and dangled, heavy and frozen. Identify the feeling.
steps: Thrashing wildly (the text's word is 'flailed') shows helpless movement.
Choking and frozen legs show physical failure.
Together they convey panic.

learn.reallife: Sports commentators use vivid sensory words, 'the ball skids, the crowd roars', to make you feel a match. Douglas does the same for drowning.

games.title: Pool or Warm Lake?
items: Legs hung as if paralysed
Tried to scream, no sound
Swallowed water and choked
Swam across and back
Shouted with joy
Fear finally gone

quiz.q: What does Douglas call the YMCA incident?
quiz.explain: He calls being thrown into the deep end his 'misadventure'.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the word with a positive event
steps: Douglas uses a word for the unlucky YMCA incident.
He calls it a 'misadventure'.
Answer: A misadventure

quiz.q: 'Flailed' in the drowning scene means
quiz.explain: To flail is to wave arms or legs wildly and helplessly.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a calm action
steps: To flail is to wave the arms or legs wildly.
So 'flailed' means moved the arms wildly.
Answer: moved the arms wildly

quiz.q: 'Vestiges of the old terror' means
options: small traces of the old fear
the cause of the old fear
quiz.explain: Vestiges are small remaining parts.
quiz.mistake: Misses the idea of 'remaining traces'
steps: Vestiges are small traces that remain.
So it means small traces of the old fear.
Answer: small traces of the old fear

quiz.q: 'Residual doubt' in the text refers to
quiz.explain: Residual means remaining; some doubt about his freedom from fear remained.
quiz.mistake: Takes residual as 'none'
steps: Residual means remaining.
So 'residual doubt' is doubt that still remained.
Answer: doubt that still remained

quiz.q: What literary quality makes the drowning scene gripping?
quiz.explain: Details of sight, breath and body plus repeated sinking create suspense.
quiz.mistake: Applies poetic devices to prose
steps: The scene uses sight, breath and body details, and repeated sinking.
So vivid sensory detail and suspense make it gripping.
Answer: Vivid sensory detail and suspense

quiz.q: What is the tone of 'Deep Water'?
quiz.explain: The adult Douglas thoughtfully looks back on his experience.
quiz.mistake: Confuses tone with the boy's emotions
steps: The adult Douglas looks back calmly on his childhood.
The tone is reflective.
Answer: Reflective

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The narrative contrasts helplessness with triumph.
Reason (R): Douglas later became a judge of the US Supreme Court.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but his later career does not explain the contrast within the narrative.
quiz.mistake: Treats biography as explanation
steps: A is true: the narrative contrasts helplessness with triumph.
R is true: Douglas later became a Supreme Court judge.
But his career does not explain that contrast, so R does not explain A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A

quiz.q: Extract (paraphrased): Rising, he opened his eyes and saw only water glowing yellow all around him. This line mainly creates
quiz.explain: Seeing only water conveys being trapped below the surface.
quiz.mistake: Reads the colour image as cheerful
steps: He sees only yellow water all around him.
This creates a sense of being trapped under the water.
Answer: a sense of being trapped

teach.ask: Gappu holds a dictionary: 'What do flailed, vestiges and misadventure mean in Deep Water?'
teach.praise: Word wizard! Flailed is waving wildly, vestiges are traces, and the misadventure is the deep-end accident.
teach.nudge: Explain at least two of the words with examples from the story.

revise.summary: Douglas's vivid sensory detail and repetition build suspense in the drowning scene, while the reflective adult voice contrasts helplessness with triumph. Key words include bruiser, flailed, misadventure, vestiges and residual.
remember: Misadventure = unlucky accident; flailed = waved wildly
Vestiges = small traces; residual = remaining
Tone: reflective
traps: 'Residual doubt' means doubt that remains, not no doubt
The tone is reflective, not comic

learn.hook: The examiner asks: 'How did the instructor build a swimmer?' You have 40 words. Ready?
points: Why he was determined: fear was ruining fishing, canoeing and outdoor joy.
How the instructor built a swimmer: belt-rope-pulley, then breathing, kicking and strokes, piece by piece.
How he tested himself: two miles at Lake Wentworth; across and back at Warm Lake.
Short answers (40–50 words) on the YMCA incident and the training method should give sequence and one key detail.
Long answer (120–150 words) on courage: cause of fear, its effects, the determined effort, the tests, and the lesson about fear itself; link to your own life.

example.q: Write a 40-word answer: How did the experience in the pool affect Douglas?
steps: Immediate effect: near drowning and blackout.
Long-term effect: a haunting fear of water for years.
Result: missed joys, then a decision to conquer it.
example.answer: Nearly drowning left Douglas with a haunting fear of water; his legs froze in any river or lake. For years he missed canoeing and fishing until he resolved to hire an instructor and overcome it.

learn.reallife: Many Olympians speak openly about stage fright and anxiety. Talking about fear, as Douglas does, helps others face theirs.

games.title: Long answer plan
games.prompt: Order a 150-word answer on overcoming fear
items: The cause: the beach and the YMCA incident
The effect: years of fear spoiling his joy
The effort: an instructor and months of training
The test: Lake Wentworth and Warm Lake
The lesson: all we have to fear is fear itself

games.title: Exam answer check
items: A good short answer on the training method mentions the rope and pulley.
That is the key detail of the method.
Douglas's tests were at the Yakima River and the YMCA pool.
His tests were at Lake Wentworth and Warm Lake.
A long answer can link Douglas's lesson to the student's own life.
Discussion questions invite personal fears overcome.
Douglas overcame his fear in a single day.
It took months of training and later tests.
The near-death experience made him value life more.
His will to live grew stronger.

quiz.q: Why was Douglas determined to get over his fear?
options: He wanted to become a lifeguard
It robbed him of the joys of outdoor life
quiz.explain: His fear kept him from canoeing, fishing and bathing in rivers he loved.
quiz.mistake: Invents an outside reason
steps: The fear stopped him from fishing, canoeing and bathing.
It robbed him of the joys of outdoor life.
Answer: It robbed him of the joys of outdoor life

quiz.q: Which phrase sums up the instructor's method best?
options: Piece by piece he built a swimmer
He threw Douglas into the lake
He showed Douglas films of swimmers
quiz.explain: The instructor broke swimming into parts and built it up gradually.
quiz.mistake: Picks a method opposite to the gradual one
steps: The instructor taught one skill at a time and joined them.
'Piece by piece he built a swimmer' sums this up.
Answer: Piece by piece he built a swimmer

quiz.q: Why did Douglas not stop after the instructor's training ended?
options: He wanted to join a swimming club
He still felt traces of terror
The instructor asked for more money
He had forgotten how to swim
quiz.explain: Vestiges of fear remained, so he kept testing himself.
quiz.mistake: Assumes training ended the fear
steps: Training ended, but fear sometimes returned when he swam alone.
He still felt traces of terror, so he kept testing himself.
Answer: He still felt traces of terror

quiz.q: How did Douglas finally know his fear was gone?
options: He swam across Warm Lake and back alone
The instructor gave him a certificate
He won a race at the YMCA pool
He saved a drowning child in a river
quiz.explain: Swimming alone across and back at Warm Lake proved it.
quiz.mistake: Imagines an external proof
steps: The final test was at Warm Lake.
He swam across and back alone and knew the fear was gone.
Answer: He swam across Warm Lake and back alone

quiz.q: Which is the best opening sentence for a long answer on courage in 'Deep Water'?
options: Courage is facing fear, not lacking it.
Douglas later became a judge in America.
The YMCA pool was about nine feet deep.
Douglas liked to fish in mountain rivers.
quiz.explain: A long answer should open with a clear thesis on the theme.
quiz.mistake: Starts with a plain fact
steps: A long answer should begin with a clear thesis on courage.
'Courage is facing fear, not lacking it' does that; the others are plain facts.
Answer: Courage is facing fear, not lacking it.

quiz.q: What does the near-death experience teach Douglas about death?
options: Death is always painful and terrible
Death has peace; the terror is in fearing it
Only weak people ever fear death
Death can always be avoided by luck
quiz.explain: He felt peace and calm; he says the terror lies in the fear of death.
quiz.mistake: Reverses his reflection
steps: Douglas felt peace near death.
He concludes death has peace; the terror is in fearing it.
Answer: Death has peace; the terror is in fearing it

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Douglas had to test himself in lakes afterwards.
Reason (R): The instructor's training was enough by itself to remove all of Douglas's fear.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: R is false: traces of fear remained. A is true; he tested himself at Lake Wentworth and Warm Lake.
quiz.mistake: Overlooks the later tests
steps: A is true: he tested himself in lakes afterwards.
R is false: traces of fear remained after training.
Answer: A is true, but R is false

quiz.q: Case: A girl who fell off a bicycle avoids cycling for years, then practises daily with her brother holding the seat until she rides alone. Which value from 'Deep Water' does she show?
quiz.explain: Like Douglas, she faces her fear with steady practice and help.
quiz.mistake: Picks a value not shown in the case
steps: She avoids cycling, then practises daily with help until she rides alone.
Like Douglas, she shows determination to overcome fear.
Answer: Determination to overcome fear

teach.ask: Gappu is preparing for boards: 'Give me three points for a long answer on how Douglas beat his fear.'
teach.praise: Board-ready! Training with the instructor, testing at the lakes, and the courage to face fear itself.
teach.nudge: Add how he trained and how he tested himself.

revise.summary: Board answers on 'Deep Water' cover why Douglas was determined, how the instructor built a swimmer, how he tested himself, and the lesson about fear. Short answers need sequence and a detail; long answers trace cause, effort and result.
focus: Planning a long answer on courage
remember: Determined because fear ruined fishing and canoeing
Tests: Lake Wentworth (two miles) and Warm Lake
Courage is facing fear, not lacking it
traps: Don't open a long answer with a plain fact
Don't say training alone ended the fear
